clue.text: Catching a famous old novelist out?

definitions.meaning: in cricket, taking catches is part of the work of the side in the field
In cricket the side that is out in the field rather than batting is doing this

explanation.surface: Someone spots a celebrated dead author venturing outdoors.
explanation.walkthrough: Cricket knowledge helps: the side not batting is 'out' in the field, and catching is one of its jobs. The second reading also names the 18th-century novelist Henry Fielding.
explanation.definitionFit: Catching the ball is a core part of cricket's outfield duties, and the eighteenth-century writer of Tom Jones bore that surname.

clue.text: Destruction of a green may provoke anger

indicators.note: destruction breaks something apart, so the letters of these two words are broken up and rebuilt

explanation.surface: Wrecking a village green is the kind of thing that makes locals furious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Destruction of' rearranges the six letters of A GREEN.
explanation.definitionFit: To madden someone or make them furious is exactly to stir up their wrath.

clue.text: One churchman in company with another

indicators.note: the abbreviation for company sits inside the word for the second churchman

parts.note: another churchman: a dean heads a cathedral chapter

explanation.surface: A clergyman is seen out and about with a fellow cleric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Another' stands for a second churchman, which is easy to miss since the definition already names one; 'in' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A deacon is an ordained minister ranking below a priest, so he is one sort of clergyman.

clue.text: Clear tone I produced is modern

indicators.note: produced suggests the letters are made into something new, here a rearrangement

explanation.surface: A singer's pure note is said to sound contemporary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Produced' signals an anagram of CLEAR TONE I, ten letters in all.
explanation.definitionFit: Neoterical is a rare word for newly introduced or recent, from Greek for newer.

clue.text: Nothing to the east of the river

parts.note: nil means nothing, as in a football score
E is the compass abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: A traveller reports there is nothing at all beyond the river's eastern bank.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue, 'to the east of' puts E after NIL.
explanation.definitionFit: The Nile is Africa's great river, flowing north through Egypt to the Mediterranean.

clue.text: A measure of the ruler

definitions.meaning: a unit in the old British system of weights such as pints and gallons
belonging to an emperor or empire

explanation.surface: A ruler's own unit of measurement is being described.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruler' tempts as a measuring stick; here it is an emperor.
explanation.definitionFit: The pre-metric British system of pints and pounds bears this name, and the adjective also means pertaining to an emperor.

clue.text: Begs hospital department, spilling tears

parts.note: ENT is the ear, nose and throat department of a hospital

indicators.note: spilling scatters things, so the letters of tears are scattered and rearranged

explanation.surface: A patient in an ear, nose and throat ward pleads, crying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spilling' signals the anagram, turning the tears of the surface into REATS; ENT is the usual crossword hospital department.
explanation.definitionFit: To beseech or implore someone is to plead earnestly, the same as begging.

clue.text: Calm water at close of day?

parts.note: even can mean calm and steady, as in an even temper
the tide is the rise and fall of the sea's water

explanation.surface: Seas are peaceful as evening falls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At' simply joins the two halves.
explanation.definitionFit: Eventide is a poetic word for evening, the time when daylight ends.

clue.text: Distant student festivity — very big — brings out huddled masses

parts.note: far means distant
in Britain a rag is a student charity carnival
OS is the clothing abbreviation for outsize

explanation.surface: A huge, far-off student party draws out a crowded throng.
explanation.walkthrough: A RAG is a British university charity week; OS (outsize) marks very large clothes. 'Huddled masses' is a jumbled heap, not a crowd.
explanation.definitionFit: A farrago is a confused mixture or hotchpotch, so these are jumbled collections lumped together.

clue.text: Confront fellow-pilot

parts.note: F is an abbreviation for fellow, as in FRS
an ace is an expert pilot, especially a fighter pilot

explanation.surface: A flier squares up to a colleague in the cockpit.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen in 'fellow-pilot' is surface glue; the two halves give F and ACE.
explanation.definitionFit: To meet a challenge or opponent head-on is to confront it.

clue.text: Two articles on species of plant bract

indicators.note: in an across clue, placed on means written after, so the articles follow the abbreviation

parts.note: SP is the standard abbreviation for species
the indefinite and definite articles, a and the
the indefinite and definite articles, a and the

explanation.surface: A botany textbook writes up a pair of papers on a kind of leafy sheath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' in an across answer means coming after, so the articles go second; 'of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A spathe is the large leafy sheath enclosing a flower cluster, as in arum lilies, which botanists class as a bract.

clue.text: Name of machine part only women use?

parts.note: a cog is a toothed wheel in a machine
with only women present there are no men

explanation.surface: Someone asks what a gadget component used solely by females is called.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Only women' means no men, read as NO MEN.
explanation.definitionFit: A cognomen is a surname or nickname, originally the third of a Roman's names, such as Caesar.

clue.text: Old city chap calling for immediate action

parts.note: Ur was an ancient Sumerian city, a crossword favourite
a gent is a gentleman or chap

explanation.surface: An ancient town's fellow cries out for prompt measures.
explanation.definitionFit: Something pressing demands to be dealt with at once.

clue.text: Movie mogul producing two versions of "the stud" and ten in between

parts.note: a stud is a decorative knob, and so is a boss; the word itself is the other version
the figures 1 and 0 written as letters, I and O, make ten
a stud is a decorative knob, and so is a boss; the word itself is the other version

explanation.surface: A film tycoon makes two films of The Stud, a racy novel, with ten others between them.
explanation.walkthrough: A boss is a raised ornamental knob, so both it and the word stud itself are versions of a stud; 'and ten in between' sets 1 and 0 between them. The Stud was a racy 1978 film.
explanation.definitionFit: A head of a film studio is a powerful Hollywood producer, the classic mogul.

clue.text: Diverted by woman's pamphlet sent to journalist

parts.note: Di's, belonging to Di, a woman's name
a tract is a short pamphlet, often religious
ED is short for editor, the stock crossword journalist

explanation.surface: Someone is sidetracked by a lady's leaflet passed to a reporter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sent to' joins the pieces in order.
explanation.definitionFit: A mind diverted from its task has had its attention drawn away elsewhere.

clue.text: Seaman will do wrong to take the drink

parts.note: AB is an able-bodied seaman
to sin is to do wrong

explanation.surface: A sailor will misbehave by taking to the bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Will', 'to take' simply join the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Absinthe is a strong green aniseed-flavoured spirit made with wormwood.

clue.text: Meant to collect fiancée

definitions.meaning: had in mind as a purpose
the person one is engaged to marry

explanation.surface: Someone planned to pick up the woman they are engaged to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To collect' only joins the two senses: meant on purpose, and the person one is engaged to.
explanation.definitionFit: Planned or purposed, and a betrothed partner, are both called by this past participle.

clue.text: Taking for granted, being arrogant

explanation.surface: Someone is presumptuous and overbearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Being' links; the second sense is the adjective meaning presumptuous.
explanation.definitionFit: Supposing without proof, and presumptuous or haughty in manner, both carry this word.

clue.text: The orchestra doesn't sit down at these venues

definitions.text: The orchestra doesn't sit down at these venues

parts.words: The orchestra doesn't sit down at these venues
parts.note: read literally, the musical group stays upright; in fact these are park pavilions where a musical group plays

explanation.surface: Musicians stay on their feet at certain concert spots.
explanation.walkthrough: Split into two words, the answer says the band stands, the joke behind the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: These are outdoor roofed platforms in parks where brass ensembles perform.

clue.text: Metal found in some major moluccan mines

indicators.note: the letters sit within part of the next two words, straddling the gap

explanation.surface: Ore is discovered in Indonesian mines in the Moluccas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Found in some' points to letters running across majOR MOLUccan.
explanation.definitionFit: Ormolu is gilded bronze or a gold-coloured alloy of copper and zinc used in decoration.

clue.text: Poem on ship heading for a port

parts.note: an ode is a lyric poem
SS stands for steamship, here a vessel bound for the next word
taken as written, the last letter

explanation.surface: Verses about a vessel bound for a harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' puts ODE above SS; the steamship is 'heading for' the A that follows it, so 'a' is taken as written.
explanation.definitionFit: Odessa is a major Black Sea harbour city in Ukraine.

clue.text: A god once worshipped in Zambia, Spain and America

parts.note: Z is the international vehicle code for Zambia
E, for España, is the vehicle code for Spain
US is short for the United States

explanation.surface: An ancient deity is said to have been revered across three countries.
explanation.walkthrough: International car registration letters give Z and E.
explanation.definitionFit: The supreme deity of Greek myth was revered in antiquity but is no longer.

clue.text: True, I'm confused again

indicators.note: confused means muddled, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone admits they are muddled, and it has happened before.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Confused' rearranges TRUE IM.
explanation.definitionFit: Iterum is Latin for a second time, used in English in formal or legal contexts.

clue.text: Time to make breakfast?

definitions.meaning: British slang for a prison sentence, as in doing time
an oat dish eaten hot in the morning

explanation.surface: Someone says it is the hour to cook the morning meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doing porridge' is British slang for serving a jail sentence; 'to make' just links.
explanation.definitionFit: A stretch in jail is British slang 'bird' or 'stir', and the oat-based morning dish shares the name.

clue.text: Iranian in Afghanistan gives a bit to Jack — one kilo

parts.note: a tad is a little bit
J is the abbreviation for jack in playing cards
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A man in Afghanistan hands a small amount to Jack, along with a kilogram.
explanation.walkthrough: Tadjik is an older spelling of Tajik; 'Iranian' means of the Iranian language family, not of Iran.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tajiks are a Persian-speaking people, many living in Afghanistan, ethnically Iranian.

clue.text: He was a big man in ancient Greece

definitions.text: He was a big man in ancient Greece

parts.words: He was a big man in ancient Greece
parts.note: seems to describe an important person, but means a huge bronze statue of Helios at Rhodes

explanation.surface: A notable figure from classical Greek history is recalled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big man' sounds like a VIP; it is literally giant, the statue that was one of the Seven Wonders.
explanation.definitionFit: The giant statue of the sun god at Rhodes was one of the Seven Wonders, and the word now means anything gigantic.

clue.text: Old Venetian can follow English

parts.note: to dog someone is to follow them closely

explanation.surface: An elderly man from Venice is able to keep up with the English.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' is the trick: it looks like part of the definition but merely joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The doge was the elected chief magistrate of the former Venetian republic.

clue.text: It could be cute also to kiss

indicators.note: could be suggests the letters might form something else when rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone thinks a smooch might be sweet as well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Could be' signals an anagram of CUTE ALSO.
explanation.definitionFit: Osculate is a formal or humorous word for kissing, from Latin osculum, little mouth.
